name: Parkinson Disease 26, Autosomal Dominant
aliases: Parkinson disease 26, autosomal dominant, susceptibility to

prevalence.estimate: Unknown; considered rare, accounting for a small subset of familial Parkinson disease.

criteria.description: Presence of parkinsonism (bradykinesia plus either rest tremor or rigidity)
Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with affected first-degree relatives
Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in LRP10 gene

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All major criteria required. Minor criteria supportive but not required.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for LRP10 variants in the context of compatible clinical and family history.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Bradykinesia with rest tremor and/or rigidity in a patient with LRP10 variant and family history

occasional.symptomName: Autonomic dysfunction (orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary symptoms)

rare.symptomName: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder

laboratory: No disease-specific laboratory abnormalities; routine labs typically normal
imaging: Dopaminergic deficit on DaTscan (reduced striatal uptake)
Normal brain MRI or mild atrophy in advanced cases
genetic: Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in LRP10 gene (heterozygous)
other: Positive family history consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance

distinguishingFeatures: May present with earlier onset and more rapid progression
LRRK2 mutations are more common and may have variable penetrance
Autosomal recessive inheritance and typically earlier onset (<40 years)

redFlags: Absence of family history or negative LRP10 genetic testing
Early onset (<40 years) or rapid progression suggesting alternative genetic forms
references: Klein C, Westenberger A. Genetics of Parkinson's Disease. Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med. 2012 Jan;2(1):a008888.
Hernandez DG, Reed X, Singleton AB. Genetics in Parkinson disease: Mendelian versus non-Mendelian inheritance. J Neurochem. 2016;139(Suppl 1):59-74.
Trinh J, Farrer M. Advances in the genetics of Parkinson disease. Nat Rev Neurol. 2013 Aug;9(8):445-54.
commonPitfalls: Assuming all familial Parkinson disease is due to LRRK2 or SNCA mutations
Overlooking LRP10 testing in familial cases with negative common gene panels
Misattributing cognitive decline to Alzheimer's disease rather than Parkinson disease
Failure to recognize autosomal dominant inheritance pattern
Relying solely on imaging without genetic confirmation

extendedDiscriminators.feature: LRP10 mutations, not SNCA; typically later onset and less rapid progression
LRP10 gene involvement; LRRK2 is more common and has variable penetrance
Autosomal dominant inheritance and later onset in PARK26 vs. autosomal recessive and early onset in PARK2

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of pathogenic or likely pathogenic LRP10 variant
No family history of parkinsonism or evidence of autosomal dominant inheritance
Presence of alternative genetic cause (e.g., SNCA, LRRK2, PARK2 mutation)
Atypical features inconsistent with Parkinson disease (e.g., prominent early cognitive decline, cerebellar signs)
